today.name: AI Context Flow MCP

Save a client brief in Claude, and tomorrow your ChatGPT, Grok Bot and your teammate’s Cursor all work from the same version. Organize memory into buckets by project or client, choose who can access each one, and see every edit in full version history. If an agent overwrites something, roll it back.

today.name: Glassmail
today.tagline: A fast Mac email app with AI that never leaves your Mac
today.description: Most new email apps charge you every month and send your mail to their servers so their AI can read it. Glassmail doesn't. yesterday.name: Currents
yesterday.tagline: Currents for Claude & Codex to see all your tests
yesterday.description: Currents records every Playwright test run in CI. Now Claude and Codex can read it. Connect from the Claude or ChatGPT/Codex plugin directory, sign in, and ask why CI failed. Your agent gets the failure, its history and the trace. Automatically.

comments.text: Hi Product Hunt! I'm Sumit from Currents.Currents records every Playwright test run in your CI: the errors, the steps, the traces, screenshots and videos, and the history of each test. Until now, people read that record in our dashboard. Now Claude and Codex can read it too.Why we built thisI watched the same loop happen again and again this year. An agent writes the code and runs the tests on its machine. It says "done". Then CI goes red on the PR, and the agent doesn't know, because it can't see CI. So a person opens the dashboard, finds the failed test and pastes the error back into the chat. The agent guesses a fix, and the loop starts again.Writing code got fast. Proving that the code works did not. The person who copies errors from CI into the chat became the slowest step.But the odd part was: Currents already had the answers. Did this test fail before this change? Does it fail only in CI? Did other tests fail with the same error? It was all in the record. But the record lived in a dashboard, and agents don't open dashboards.So we spent the last few months on the agent side of Currents. We shipped a hosted MCP server with OAuth sign-in. We shipped a Trace API, so an agent can read a Playwright trace one piece at a time. In our launch example, that took 4 calls and about 1,600 tokens. Every file in that trace comes to about 20,000.The last gap was setup. An MCP server helps nobody if people can't find it, or if they first have to copy a server URL and an API key into a config file. So we listed Currents in the Claude directory and in the ChatGPT/Codex plugin directory. You find it, click connect and sign in.What you can ask"What broke in the last failed run on main? Open a Jira issue for it.""Which tests were flakiest on main this week, and why?""Is this pull request safe to merge? Compare its runs with main."The plugin also brings three skills:fix-failing-tests finds the failed run, reads each failure with its steps and trace, fixes the cause, runs the test again and asks before it commits.collect-evidence finds the run before your change and the run after it, and writes up both with links.browser-evidence (experimental) records the browser before and after a change and shares the link.You act as yourself, so your Currents role decides what the agent can do.Who it's forTeams that run Playwright in CI and work with Claude, Claude Code, ChatGPT or Codex. Currents has a 14-day free trial, and you don't need a credit card.What I'd love from youTry it, and tell me where it broke or where it confused you. yesterday.name: Kuc-kuc
yesterday.tagline: A knock on the door when dangerous weather comes
yesterday.description: When dangerous weather is forecast, Kuc-kuc phones an older person who lives alone and asks if they are okay. No answer, or “I’m not well”? It phones a neighbour to go and knock. The family sees every step. Works on a landline. Runs on Cloud Run.

comments.text: Hi Product Hunt! "Kuc-kuc" is Serbian for "knock-knock".My grandmother lives alone in a village in southern Serbia. She has a landline, no smartphone, and a neighbour across the road. Her family is far away. Heatwaves and hard frosts are when we worry most, and exactly when nobody remembers to call.What it does. Every three hours Kuc-kuc reads the forecast for each person's village. When heat, frost, wind or snow crosses a threshold, it phones them the evening before with a warning, and on the day itself with one question: are you all right? They answer out loud, on any phone. If they don't pick up, or say they're not well, it phones the neighbour and asks them to go and knock, then calls the neighbour back 20 minutes later to ask how she is. The family sees every step on a web page and on Telegram. One rule runs through all of it: any doubt counts as a problem, never as "fine". And a forecast never rings anyone's phone before 08:00 or after 20:00 their time.Try it. The demo on the site calls your own phone, in English. Don't pick up, and a moment later it calls you back as the neighbour.How it is built on Cloud Run. Three services, all scaling to zero:web: the site, the live demo and the family page.engine: private (internal ingress only), one pure state machine. It does nothing but react to events from Pub/Sub and timers from Cloud Tasks.voice: the only code that touches the phone network. It speaks with a Chirp 3 HD voice (Serbian and English) and sends the recorded answer to Gemini on Vertex AI, which tells "I'm fine" from "I'm not well" from "unclear".Plus Cloud Run jobs: forecast-scan, started by Cloud Scheduler every three hours; watchdog, every ten minutes, which closes any check that has stopped moving and tells the family at once, so a lost message never turns into silence; and loadtest. Services never call each other: every event goes through Pub/Sub, and every wait ("call again in 10 minutes", "ask the neighbour in 20") is a Cloud Tasks task, so nothing stays awake waiting. State lives in Firestore, recordings in Cloud Storage (deleted after 7 days), secrets in Secret Manager.Why scale to zero. Dangerous weather is rare. On an ordinary day there is nothing to do, so nothing runs. Our load test put 2,000 simulated people in a heatwave at once: 3,008 simulated calls, every case closed in 213 seconds at a peak of 14 instances, and then everything went back to zero.Limits, said plainly. It is not an emergency service. It is a pilot by invitation, because every call costs real money. Its first real user is my grandmother.The Architecture page on the site shows all of this, live.

comments.text: Hey Product Hunt,I'm Ravi, co-founder of Scalekit. Today we're launching AgentKit, an MCP gateway that handles auth and tool-calling for AI agents in production.Why now? Over the last year, wiring an agent to a tool got easy. MCP standardized the interface, and any agent can now call Gmail or Salesforce after an afternoon of work.But the tool call is only the surface. Once an agent ships to real users, everything underneath it shows up:whose credentials each call executes withwhich tools each agent should have in contextthe internal systems no catalog coverswhat happens when an upstream API pushes backwho's accountable for every actionThat layer decides whether an agent makes it to production. It's what we built AgentKit for.Try it free: scalekit.com. The free tier includes 10,000 tool calls a month and all 600+ connectors. Make your first tool call from the dashboard, or start from your terminal with npx @ scalekit-inc/cli setup.Here's what it looks like in practice.Say you're shipping a sales agent inside your product. A rep types: "Prep me for the Acme renewal. Pull the deal, the last three email threads, what the team said in Slack, when we last met them, and how much they've used the product this quarter."Four apps, one ask. Getting it working for one rep in a demo is easy. Here's what's underneath when it runs for every rep at every customer:Thousands of OAuth grants, not four. 40 customers × 30 reps × Salesforce, Gmail, Slack and Calendar = 4,800 connected accounts. Each needs its tokens stored, isolated per customer, and refreshed before they expire mid-run. → AgentKit manages connected accounts end to end. Users authorize through an auth link you surface in your app. Tokens live in a per-tenant AES-256 vault, refresh automatically, and are injected at execution time. They never touch your code, logs, or prompts.Every call has to execute as the right user. The agent should see what that rep can see at that customer, and nothing more. Not a shared service account with org-wide access to every inbox. → Every tool call executes with the end user's own credentials, within the scopes they granted.Every tool definition costs context. Gmail alone exposes ~30 tools; four apps put over a hundred on the table. At ~200 tokens per definition, 40 tools burn ~8,000 tokens before the agent does any work, and tool selection gets worse as the list grows. Your prep agent needs about ten tools. Your outbound agent needs a different ten. → Virtual MCP Servers let you compose a tool set per agent role, across connectors. Each role gets one static MCP URL; you mint a short-lived session token per user per run. Smaller context and least-privilege access: ten tool definitions (~2,000 tokens) instead of over a hundred (20,000+).The data you need has no connector. Usage lives in your customer's internal analytics service. No catalog covers it, so you'd build that integration yourself, auth included. → Define it as a custom connector (OAuth 2.0, API key, bearer token, RSA or basic auth), or point AgentKit at a remote MCP server. It runs on the same gateway with the same credential handling and logs as the 600+ built-in connectors.It has to hold up and be auditable. Rate limits, timeouts, upstream errors the model can't act on. Then a deal stage changes and someone asks whether the rep did it or the agent did. → Retries and rate limits are handled on every call. Every call is logged with agent, user, tool and response, and logs stream to Datadog or Splunk.None of this shows up in a demo. All of it shows up in production. AgentKit handles that layer: 30,000+ tools across 600+ apps behind one MCP gateway. And with Triggers, an agent can start on its own the moment an email lands.Python and Node SDKs. Works with the Anthropic and OpenAI SDKs, LangChain, Google ADK, Vercel AI SDK, Mastra, and Claude Code. You keep your framework and backend.Which of these five has slowed your agent down the most?
